\chapter{Graphs And Subgraphs}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Graphs And Subgraphs}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.GraphsAndSubgraphs.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{theorem}[nonempty\_iso\_iff]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nonempty_iso_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.nonempty_iso_iff}
\leanok
B\&M's general isomorphism needs two bijections, one on vertices and one
on edges, respecting incidence.  For \emph{simple} graphs the edge bijection carries no
information --- at most one edge joins any pair --- so an adjacency-preserving vertex
bijection already induces it.  This is precisely why Mathlib can define $G $\simeq$g H$ as
an equivalence of vertex types with \texttt{G.Adj u v $\leftrightarrow$ H.Adj ($\theta$ u) ($\theta$ v)}, and this
exercise is the justification for using it throughout the file.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[edgeCard\_eq\_choose\_two\_iff\_top]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeCard_eq_choose_two_iff_top}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeCard_eq_choose_two_iff_top}
\leanok
Exercise 1.1.3 gives $\varepsilon \le C(\nu,2)$; equality means the injection from
edges to pairs is \emph{onto}, i.e. every pair carries an edge --- the definition of
complete.

"Complete" is $G = \top$, the top of the lattice of simple graphs
on $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[completeBipartite\_edgeCard]
\lean{SimpleGraph.completeBipartite_edgeCard}
\label{SimpleGraph.completeBipartite_edgeCard}
\leanok
$K_{m,n}$ contains exactly one edge for each choice of a vertex in $X$
and one in $Y$, so edges biject with $X \times Y$.

The carrier is \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ Fin n}, so "opposite sides" is a \texttt{Sum}
case split; step 1's well-definedness is the only fiddly point.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[bipartite\_edgeCard\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bipartite_edgeCard_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.bipartite_edgeCard_le}
\leanok
$mn$ with fixed sum $\nu$ is largest when the parts are equal, giving
$\nu^{2}/4$; the bound is attained by $K_{\nu/2,\nu/2}$.

Stated in the cleared form $4\varepsilon \le \nu^{2}$ to stay in $\mathbb{N}$, and
bipartiteness as \texttt{Colorable 2} --- Mathlib's \texttt{IsBipartite} is an abbreviation for
exactly that.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Ex 1.2.10: the $k$-cube --- vertices are $k$-bit strings, adjacent iff they differ in exactly one coordinate]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
\label{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
\leanok
Each vertex is a binary string of length $k$, equivalently a corner of a
$k$-dimensional cube; two corners are joined when their descriptions agree everywhere
but one position.  For $k = 3$ this is literally the corners and edges of an ordinary
cube --- the book's figure 1.4b.

Mathlib has no named hypercube graph, so this is built here.
Tuples are \texttt{Fin k $\to$ Bool}; "differ in exactly one coordinate" is $\exists! i, x i \ne y i$.
\texttt{SimpleGraph.fromRel} symmetrises the relation and removes the diagonal, which is
what makes the result a \texttt{SimpleGraph} without a separate looplessness proof --- at the
cost that \texttt{Adj} unfolds to $x \ne y \land (R x y \lor R y x)$, as the \texttt{hypercube\_bipartite}
proof has to unpack.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[hypercube\_edgeCard]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hypercube_edgeCard}
\label{SimpleGraph.hypercube_edgeCard}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
Every vertex has degree $k$, one neighbour per coordinate flip.

\textbf{!} $k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction; the $k = 0$ case is where it bites,
and it happens to come out right, but only by accident of $0 * _ = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[hypercube\_bipartite]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hypercube_bipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.hypercube_bipartite}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
Split the tuples by the parity of their number of $1$s; an edge flips
exactly one entry and so changes that parity, making every edge cross between the
classes.

Bipartiteness as \texttt{Colorable 2}, with \texttt{ZMod 2} as the palette and
\texttt{simpa} bridging to \texttt{Fin 2}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[selfComplementary\_card\_mod\_four]
\lean{SimpleGraph.selfComplementary_card_mod_four}
\label{SimpleGraph.selfComplementary_card_mod_four}
\leanok
Self-complementary means $G \cong G^{c}$, so $G$ has exactly half of all
possible edges --- which forces $\nu \equiv 0$ or \texttt{1 (mod 4)}.  The smallest examples are the
path $P_{4}$ ($\nu = 4$) and the cycle $C_{5}$ ($\nu = 5$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[induce\_completeGraph]
\lean{SimpleGraph.induce_completeGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.induce_completeGraph}
\leanok
$G[V']$ keeps $V'$ and \emph{all} edges of $G$ with both ends there.  If $G$
is complete, every pair inside $V'$ is joined and every such edge is retained --- so
$G[V']$ is complete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[subgraph\_bipartite]
\lean{SimpleGraph.subgraph_bipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.subgraph_bipartite}
\leanok
Every edge of $H$ is an edge of $G$, so the very same bipartition still
has every edge crossing: deleting vertices and edges can never create an edge inside
a part.

Stated for $H \le G$ on the \emph{same} carrier, which is the
spanning-subgraph case.  B\&M's "subgraph" also allows dropping vertices; that case is
\texttt{induce\_bipartite} and the two together are \texttt{subgraph\_induce\_bipartite}, both below.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[induce\_bipartite]
\lean{SimpleGraph.induce_bipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.induce_bipartite}
\leanok
\texttt{subgraph\_bipartite} covers B\&M's \emph{spanning} subgraphs (same vertex set,
fewer edges); this covers the other half of what B\&M call a subgraph --- throwing
vertices away.  Restricting a bipartition to a vertex subset still leaves every
surviving edge crossing.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[subgraph\_induce\_bipartite]
\lean{SimpleGraph.subgraph_induce_bipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.subgraph_induce_bipartite}
\leanok
This is the exercise as the book states it; \texttt{subgraph\_bipartite}
(edges only) and \texttt{induce\_bipartite} (vertices only) are the two halves, and either
alone is what a Lean transcription tends to produce.  \textbf{!} Nothing in the proof uses
$2$ specifically; the identical two lines give the \texttt{Colorable k} statement for any
$k$, should a general version be wanted.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[sum\_degrees\_eq\_two\_mul\_edgeCard]
\lean{SimpleGraph.sum_degrees_eq_two_mul_edgeCard}
\label{SimpleGraph.sum_degrees_eq_two_mul_edgeCard}
\leanok
Adding up the degrees counts each edge twice, once from each end.  The
name comes from the reading: if each edge is a handshake, the total hands shaken is
twice the number of handshakes.  Loops are consistent, contributing $2$ to their
single end.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[even\_card\_odd\_degree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.even_card_odd_degree}
\label{SimpleGraph.even_card_odd_degree}
\leanok
A sum of odd numbers is even precisely when there is an even number of
terms.  This tiny corollary is what \S{}1.9 uses to derive Sperner's lemma, and through
it Brouwer's fixed-point theorem --- the chapter's most striking application.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[degree\_bounds]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degree_bounds}
\label{SimpleGraph.degree_bounds}
\leanok
$2\varepsilon/\nu$ is the \emph{average} degree, since the degrees sum to $2\varepsilon$ and there
are $\nu$ of them; an average lies between the extremes.

Stated multiplicatively to avoid division: $\nu\cdot\delta \le 2\varepsilon \le \nu\cdot\Delta$.
\texttt{[Nonempty V]} keeps \texttt{minDegree}/\texttt{maxDegree} meaningful --- both are \texttt{sInf}/\texttt{sSup}-like
and degenerate on an empty carrier.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[regular\_bipartite\_card\_eq]
\lean{SimpleGraph.regular_bipartite_card_eq}
\label{SimpleGraph.regular_bipartite_card_eq}
\leanok
Count the edges twice, once from each side.  \textbf{!} $hk : 0 < k$ is
essential --- a $0$-regular graph has no edges and its two parts can have any sizes.

\texttt{IsBipartiteWith s t} is Mathlib's explicit-bipartition form,
stronger than \texttt{Colorable 2} and what step 1 needs.  \texttt{Set.ncard} rather than
\texttt{Finset.card}, so no decidability on $s$, $t$ is required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_bipartite\_spanning\_subgraph]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_bipartite_spanning_subgraph}
\leanok
Split the vertices in two and keep only the crossing edges --- automatically
bipartite and spanning --- choosing the split to maximise crossings.  Then no vertex can
have more than half its edges inside its own part, or moving it would improve the
split.

Conclusion in the cleared form $d_G(v) \le 2 d_H(v)$ to stay in $\mathbb{N}$.
\textbf{!} Step 3's $i - c \le 0$ must be argued in $\mathbb{Z}$ or by \texttt{Nat.le\_of\_add\_le\_add}, not by
$\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[lineGraph\_edgeCard]
\lean{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_edgeCard}
\label{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_edgeCard}
\leanok
Two edges are adjacent in the edge graph exactly when they share an end;
simplicity makes that end unique, so the count localises at each vertex.

\textbf{!} Step 1's uniqueness is where \emph{simplicity} is spent --- with
parallel edges two edges could share both ends and be counted twice.  Part (b) of the
exercise, not stated here, notes the edge graph of $K_{5}$ is the complement of the
Petersen graph.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_path\_length\_of\_minDegree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_path_length_of_minDegree}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_path_length_of_minDegree}
\leanok
A longest path cannot be extended, so its endpoint's neighbours are all
already on it, forcing it to be long.  \textbf{!} Simplicity is what makes the $\delta$ neighbours
$\delta$ \emph{distinct} vertices --- and \texttt{SimpleGraph} supplies it for free.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[connected\_iff\_forall\_partition\_edge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.connected_iff_forall_partition_edge}
\label{SimpleGraph.connected_iff_forall_partition_edge}
\leanok
Connectivity is exactly the statement that $V$ admits no non-trivial cut
with no edges across it.

The partition is a set $s$ with its complement, both required
nonempty --- equivalent to B\&M's $(V_{1}, V_{2})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[connected\_of\_edgeCard\_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.connected_of_edgeCard_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.connected_of_edgeCard_gt}
\leanok
A disconnected simple graph is sparsest-constrained in the most lopsided
split.  The bound is \textbf{sharp}: part (b), not stated here, asks for a disconnected
simple graph with exactly $C(\nu-1,2)$ edges --- $K_{\nu-1}$ plus one isolated vertex.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[compl\_connected\_of\_not\_connected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.compl_connected_of_not_connected}
\label{SimpleGraph.compl_connected_of_not_connected}
\leanok
Every pair is joined in $G^{c}$ by a path of length at most $2$, so $G^{c}$ is
connected --- indeed of diameter $\le 2$.  Equivalently: \textbf{at least one of $G$, $G^{c}$ is
always connected}.

\textbf{!} Steps 2--3 need $u \ne w$ and $v \ne w$, which follow from them being
in different components; and "different components" must be extracted from
\texttt{$\lnot$ Connected} --- \texttt{Preconnected} failing gives an unreachable pair.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[card\_connectedComponent\_le\_of\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_connectedComponent_le_of_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_connectedComponent_le_of_le}
\leanok
If $H \le K$ then
$\omega(K) \le \omega(H)$ --- adding edges can only merge components.

Not a book statement.  This is the general lemma that exercise
1.6.8(a) below is the single-edge instance of, and it is extracted here because
\texttt{Trees.lean}'s skeleton for corollary 2.7 asks for it by name: *"the monotonicity
$H \le K \to \omega(K) \le \omega(H)$ is used here and is worth a standalone lemma --- chapter 1's
exercise 1.6.8(a) needs the same fact."*  Both call sites are served by this one
declaration.

Stated with \texttt{Nat.card}, matching \texttt{Trees.numComponents}, so that no
\texttt{DecidableEq} on the quotient is needed.  \textbf{!} Exercise 1.6.8(a) below uses
\texttt{Fintype.card}; over a \texttt{Fintype} carrier the two agree by \texttt{Nat.card\_eq\_fintype\_card},
but the transfer must be written explicitly at the call site.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[components\_deleteEdge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.components_deleteEdge}
\label{SimpleGraph.components_deleteEdge}
\leanok
Deleting an edge only destroys connections, never creates them; and it
affects only the component containing $e$, which can break into at most the parts
reachable from each end.  An edge whose deletion \emph{does} raise the count is a \textbf{cut
edge}, the subject of \S{}2.3.  \textbf{!} Part (b), not stated here, notes the analogue fails for
\emph{vertex} deletion --- removing one vertex can create many components.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[compl\_diam\_lt\_of\_diam\_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.compl_diam_lt_of_diam_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.compl_diam_lt_of_diam_gt}
\leanok
A graph and its complement cannot both be "spread out": if $G$ is very
stretched, $G^{c}$ must be very compact.

\textbf{!} \texttt{G.diam} is $\mathbb{N}$-valued and Mathlib returns $0$ for a
disconnected graph, so \texttt{3 < G.diam} silently carries "$G$ is connected" --- worth
making explicit before relying on step 1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_induced\_path\_of\_connected\_not\_complete]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_induced_path_of_connected_not_complete}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_induced_path_of_connected_not_complete}
\leanok
A connected non-complete graph always contains an induced path on three
vertices --- adjacency is transitive only when the graph is a disjoint union of complete
graphs.  \textbf{*} Consumed by Brooks' theorem 8.4, whose 3-connected case opens by invoking
exactly this.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[bipartite\_iff\_no\_odd\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bipartite_iff_no_odd_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.bipartite_iff_no_odd_cycle}
\leanok
Odd cycles are the sole obstruction to $2$-colourability --- the fact that
makes chapter 8 turn on odd cycles throughout.

Bipartiteness as \texttt{G.Colorable 2}; Mathlib's
\texttt{two\_colorable\_iff\_forall\_loop\_even} is an equivalent \emph{loop}-based form and may close
this more directly than the cycle form.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[edge\_in\_cycle\_of\_closed\_trail]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edge_in_cycle_of_closed_trail}
\label{SimpleGraph.edge_in_cycle_of_closed_trail}
\leanok
A closed trail may revisit vertices, so it need not be a cycle; the
claim is that it can be pared down to one through any chosen edge.  \textbf{!} The analogous
statement for \emph{walks} is \textbf{false} --- a walk may traverse the same edge back and forth
with no cycle present --- which is why \texttt{ht : c.IsTrail} (distinct edges) is a hypothesis
and not decoration.

\texttt{hpos : 0 < c.length} excludes the trivial closed walk, for which
$he$ would be unsatisfiable anyway but which would otherwise complicate step 1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_cycle\_of\_minDegree\_ge\_two]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_cycle_of_minDegree_ge_two}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_cycle_of_minDegree_ge_two}
\leanok
If every vertex offers a second way out you can never get stuck, so
walking forward must eventually revisit a vertex, and the first revisit closes a
cycle.  \textbf{*} Contrapositively, \textbf{an acyclic graph always has a vertex of degree $\le$ 1} ---
used repeatedly in chapter 2's theory of trees, and by chapter 12's lemma 12.2.1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_long\_cycle\_of\_minDegree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_long_cycle_of_minDegree}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_long_cycle_of_minDegree}
\leanok
Sharpens exercise 1.7.2 from "some cycle exists" to a length bound: a
graph in which every vertex has many neighbours cannot consist only of short cycles.
\textbf{*} This is chapter 10's exercise 10.1.7 one dimension down --- the directed version bounds
directed cycles by \texttt{max\{$\delta^{-}$,$\delta^{+}$\} + 1} and is used inside Ghouila-Houri's theorem 10.4.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[girth\_four\_regular\_card\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.girth_four_regular_card_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.girth_four_regular_card_ge}
\leanok
\textbf{!} B\&M add that, up to isomorphism, there is exactly \textbf{one} such graph on
$2k$ vertices, namely $K_{k,k}$; only the counting half is stated here, and the
uniqueness half would be a substantially harder separate result.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[girth\_five\_regular\_card\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.girth_five_regular_card_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.girth_five_regular_card_ge}
\leanok
Graphs attaining this bound with diameter two are the \textbf{Moore graphs}
of exercise 1.7.5; Hoffman and Singleton showed they exist only for $k = 2, 3, 7$ and
possibly $57$.  The case $k = 3$ is the \textbf{Petersen graph} --- the same graph chapter 9
uses as its counterexample to Tait's approach.

\textbf{!} $k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction; $k = 0$ makes the statement $1 \le \nu$
and \texttt{girth = 5} unsatisfiable, so the degenerate case is vacuous --- but check it rather
than assume it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists\_cycle\_of\_edgeCard\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_cycle_of_edgeCard_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_cycle_of_edgeCard_ge}
\leanok
Each edge added to a forest either joins two different components ---
possible at most $\nu - 1$ times --- or joins two already-connected vertices, immediately
closing a cycle.  \textbf{!} Part (b), due to P\'osa and not stated here, strengthens this:
$\varepsilon \ge \nu + 4$ forces two \textbf{edge-disjoint} cycles.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Hypothesis repaired.}  Step 2 needs $\omega \ge 1$, i.e.
\texttt{Nonempty V}.  Without it the statement is \textbf{false} on an empty carrier, where
$\nu = \varepsilon = 0$ so $h$ holds vacuously while no cycle exists (indeed no vertex $v$ exists
to base one at).  \texttt{[Nonempty V]} has been added; it is not in B\&M only because the
book's graphs are nonempty by convention.
\end{theorem}
